title: 172 Impact of late-gestation chromium propionate supplementation of Brangus cows on growth and liver transcriptomics of the offspring
content:
Abstract
Our objective was to evaluate the effects of late-gestation chromium (CR) supplementation of beef cows on growth and liver transcriptomics of the offspring. Twenty-four multiparous Brangus cows [6.3 ± 2.45 yr of age; body condition score (BCS) = 5.5 ± 0.88; body weight (BW) = 603 ± 65.8 kg] were assigned to 1 of 2 treatments (3 cows/pasture; 4 pasture/treatment): 1) control (no CR) or 2) CR. The CR propionate (KemTRACE Chromium 0.4%, Kemin Industries) was added to the free-choice mineral supplement (mineral target intake of 113 g/head/d) at a rate of 1.6% (CR target intake of 6.3 mg/cow/d) and was offered from d -94 to calving (d 0). After calving, all animals were allocated to a single pasture and received the control mineral until weaning (d 214). Cows BW and BCS were collected on d -94, -29, 39, 81, 151, 186, and 214, and liver biopsies on d -94 and -29. Calves BW were collected on d 0, 81, 151, 186, and 214, and liver biopsies on d 0. Liver samples were used for CR concentration analysis. In addition, liver biopsies from a subset of female calves (n = 7/treatment) were taken on d 0 for transcriptomic analysis. After quality control, the reads were mapped to the Bos taurus reference genome using STAR aligner, and differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using DESeq2. The free-choice mineral intake was similar between control and CR treatments (60.6 and 55.8 ± 8.49 g/cow/d; P = 0.71) and the CR intake was approximately 3.11 mg/cow/day. The CR supplementation tended to increase (P = 0.10) the BW and CR concentration in the liver of cows on d -29 but did not affect (P ≥ 0.21) BCS. Maternal CR supplementation increased (P = 0.03) the BW from d 81 to 214 of offspring but did not affect (P = 0.80) their CR concentration in the liver. However, transcriptomics analysis revealed 638 DEGs between the female CR and control groups (P ≤ 0.05 and |Log2FC| > 0.5). Among them, 296 genes were upregulated, and 342 were downregulated in the female CR-treated calves. Among them, the CREB3L3 gene was upregulated in the CR calves. This gene encodes a transcription factor that plays a key role in lipid and glucose metabolism in the liver. Additionally, it can act on the insulin resistance pathway. Additional over-represented KEGG pathways included FoxO signaling and glutathione metabolism. Likewise, biological processes included positive regulation of developmental processes and tissue development, which included genes such as TGFB3 and SMAD7. Our findings suggest maternal chromium supplementation during late gestation enhances prepartum cow body weight and promotes offspring growth through weaning while influencing the expression of hepatic genes in offspring at the neonatal stage.
